     decisions P58 and P59): the records of the rows are one reader of the
     labels the `lift` read, and a label is formed again also where a value
     changed with it. The branches of milestones 2 and 4 do not have it.
358. **The cost of labeling every row again in one commit** (not for the
     owner). The first create after a load on Topics' `main` takes 15.5 s at
     1,000 topics, since a new clause enters what the whole-list `lift`s read.
     *Assumed:* the preparation indexes the cleared existence entries by path,
     and no record is given for a row whose value and whose inputs' label
     identifiers are those of the run before. The second half is built on the
     branch of milestone 3 (provisional decision P59). It serves a create by a
     handler as well, since the first derivation of the created instance is
     committed before the `lift`s read it (provisional decision P64). The first
     half is not built, and the board `main` was not measured on the runner path
     after the first round.
359. **What a read through a handle depends on** (not for the owner). It
     records the root of the member's document, so a `lift` that reads two
     fields of each member runs again on a change of any field. *Assumed:* the
     positions read. Built on the branch of milestone 3 (provisional
     decisions P56 and P57): the plan holds the schema of the type a body
     declares for a handle, a read under it registers the members that schema
     declares, and the read of a container for its members reads no member.
     An edit of a title on the boards `filing-order` and `sorted-references`
     runs no whole-list `lift`.
360. **Whether every read of a position joins the `*` entry of the ruling
     Z71** (for the owner, to revisit after the main track, beside question
     352). The owner's remark of 2026-11-22 on reading the ruling again: "any
     read is joined with * - seems quite strong now that i read this. i can
     see where it comes from and it probably means we want to treat these as
     unordered sets (as that's the usual use-case) where the position doesn't
     mean much." It is a remark and no ruling; Z71 stands. The coordinator's
     analysis, not the owner's: a removal through a handle from an array of
     plain values in place decides which member stands at an index, the count
     and whether the removed member exists; it does not decide the content of
     a kept member found by its identity, nor the relative order of two kept
     members. A narrower rule would be that a read by key does not join the
     entry, and a read by index, the count and an enumeration do (the
     enumeration entry of P39 carries it already). For an array of references
     this nearly holds, since the label is on the link at the position and
     the content is in the member's document. For an array of plain values in
     place the executor keys elements and binds a row of a `map` by key, but
     today's runtime reads by index, so its label resolution cannot tell the
     two reads apart; that is the missing piece. For the result of another
     per-element construct there is no handle to remove through. A narrower
     rule changes the sentence proposed for section 4.6.3 of the
     specification's chapter on label representation (question 326).
     *Assumed* until then: Z71 as ruled.

**From milestone 3 of the integration (2026-11-22).** A compiled piece runs in
the runner behind the experimental option, for one writer on emulated storage
([compiled-pattern-language-integration.md](compiled-pattern-language-integration.md),
"Milestone 3: a compiled piece in the runner"). Questions 347, 351 and 356 to
359 above are brought in line with it. The provisional decisions P50 to P66 are
of its three rounds. Whenever a question says `map`, it names the case.

361. **The executor as a workspace package, and a build of the crate in
     continuous integration** (not for the owner; provisional decision P50).
     `base/pattern-compiler` is no workspace member, so `deno task
     check-dependency-direction` and `deno task check-package-cycles` do not see
     the import from `runtime/runner/src/compiled/` to `exec/`, nor the import
     from `compare/` to the runner. The tests of the runner path load the
     checked-in artifacts of `compare/fixtures/`, and no job builds the crate,
     so an artifact can fall behind the crate unseen. *Assumed:* `exec/` becomes
     the member `@commonfabric/pattern-executor`, `compare/` moves beside the
     runner's benchmarks, and a job builds the crate and compares the artifacts.
     Not built.
362. **What of the design's scheduler the runner path leaves out** (not for the
     owner; provisional decisions P51 to P53 and P55). The derivation of a piece
     is one scheduler action and not a node for each cone instance; an event is
     held by the scheduler's queue, with no stream document and no watermark;
     the executor's transactions within one call of the scheduler are one
     transaction of the runtime; an effect's request leaves through nothing; and
     an event that the executor refuses aborts the scheduler's transaction,
     which the scheduler drops as a rejection that running again cannot resolve.
     The derivation behind a batch is two transactions where a handler made an
     instance, which is question 373. *Assumed:* the figures of milestones 3 and
     6 are of the arrangement as built. Milestone 6 runs the piece under the
     serving loop with the same arrangement and builds none of them (question
     435). *Open:* whether one transaction for a request and the derivation
     behind it changes a stored label against a transaction for each, for a path
     that has no write record and takes the join; not examined.
363. **Where the boundary of rows as documents is decided** (not for the owner;
     provisional decision P54; beside question 356). The executor's package
     reads it from the plan when the piece starts. The integration plan has the
     compiler decide it per construct from the two templates. *Assumed:* the
     crate emits it as a member of the collection, and `rowDocumentCollections`
     goes. *Open with it:* the document of a row that left is deleted in the
     transaction that removes its link, and a reader that held the link reads
     nothing; whether such a row is kept for a time is not decided.
364. **Three over-labels found on the runner path** (not for the owner until
     examined; a fourth is question 375). First, with rows in place: an edit
     that writes below `$UI` in the result document removes the entries stored
     at `$UI` and at `$UI/children`, and a read below `$UI` with no nearer entry
     then consumes the entry of the root, which holds every clause the load
     read; found at 134 and 105 probes of two Topics boards of 4 topics. Rows as
     documents, the default, do not have it. Second, with rows as documents: a
     result that holds nothing but links is taken by the runtime for a structure
     of links, which stores for every child of its root the join of the
     transaction that wrote it, so every read below the root consumes every
     clause. Third, in the crate: a `value` slot at each member beside a handle,
     from a helper that tests a member for presence, stays in the template of
     `crossrefTable` and `namesTable`, so the label of each row holds the label
     of a read of each topic whole. *Assumed:* none is an under-label. The first
     is a defect of how a write below a path replaces the entries at it, to be
     examined with question 356. For the second the plan is that the adapter
     gives the record of the array for each link position of such a result, as
     `#recordAppended` of `runtime/runner/src/compiled/transactions.ts` does for
     the links an append adds; it may need a sentence of the specification. The
     third is the crate's to narrow, by not listing a `value` slot where the
     body is handed a handle and the read is a test for presence. None of the
     three is changed on the branch of milestone 3.
365. **A change of the members of an array of row documents** (not for the
     owner; provisional decision P60). An addition at the end writes the number
     of members and one link. A prepend and a removal write the array of links
     whole, `N` links, because the record of a change of the members of a kept
     `map` names the array and the runtime refuses a record that names a path
     the transaction did not write. This is a `map` over an array declared as
     references, or over the result of a construct that yields references. The
     storage has a mergeable append and no splice that keeps the label entries
     of the positions that stay, so a prepend or a removal has to write each
     position behind the change. *Assumed:* as built. *The plan, not built:* a
     splice operation of the storage that moves the label entries with their
     positions, as the plan-write `moves` does for a handler's splice of a
     stored list. *Open:* the records of a change of members in place
     (`PlanWrite.enumeration` with `moves`), whose label is the `enumerate`
     entry and labels no member; whether an entry at the position of a link
     added at the end, which stays until the array is next written at or above
     it, is read rightly after a later prepend; and the comparison of the
     members before and after a change by another writer, which is linear in the
     array.
366. **A write by another writer to a derived array** (not for the owner;
     provisional decision P61). It is not applied to the executor in either
     layout. With rows as documents it is reported; with rows in place nothing
     reports it. The storage then holds what the other writer wrote and the
     executor holds what it derived. *Assumed:* the piece writes the array again
     from what it holds at its next derivation, with the record of the array, in
     both layouts. Not built. It has to be closed before two writers share a
     space.
367. **What is not verified after a refused commit** (not for the owner;
     provisional decision P62). A handler that the scheduler runs again after a
     conflict was not driven through the scheduler in a test, since with the
     server's fan-out held the scheduler's wait for the replica has no end. A
     refused commit of a transaction that created an instance is not tested. A
     refused commit of the transaction a load in bounded transactions was handed
     is question 374. The work after a refusal follows the size of the result,
     since the result document is stored again row by row. What a reader of the
     replica sees between a commit and its refusal is what any optimistic write
     of the runtime shows. *Assumed:* the restore as built is sound for the
     documents a refused transaction wrote; the two cases are tested before two
     writers share a space, and the withdrawal of one derived write, which
     milestone 6 does not build, replaces the restore of the whole result. Under
     the serving loop a rejected wave is taken as a refused commit (P135;
     question 418).
368. **Whether the start of a piece may be several commits** (for the owner;
     provisional decision P65). The load of a compiled piece commits the
     documents the instance makes for itself, and then the rows that are
     documents in transactions of at most 250 rows, before the transaction the
     caller handed, which holds the result with the links and everything else.
     The design's documents have one transaction for a creation outside a
     handler (`execution-and-storage.md` §1.1, assumed there under its question
     77). *What several commits give:* the load of the Topics board
     `filing-order` at 2,000 topics is 18 commits and takes 7.5 s; in one commit
     it holds 8,011 documents and the memory server refuses it
     (`MessageTooLargeError`). *What a reader can observe in between:* the
     argument, the empty result and the state documents of the instance before a
     result links to rows, and row documents that nothing links to yet, each
     under the label it has when the load is done; no reader reaches a row by a
     link before the handed transaction commits. *What it leaves:* where the
     handed transaction is not committed or is refused, the earlier commits stay
     stored and nothing removes them; and the documents a `lift` writes for its
     rows stay in the handed transaction, so a board of about 4,000 topics is
     refused again (question 374). *The alternative:* one commit, with the limit
     of the memory server raised for it, which `CompiledPieceOptions.loadRows`
     set to `Infinity` gives; it over-labels what is bound through the argument
     (question 375). *The coordinator's recommendation, not a ruling:* several
     commits, as built. *Assumed* until answered: P65 as built.
369. **The memory server follows the links of a written document under the
     schema of the query that reached it** (not for the owner; the plan is for
     `runtime/memory`). `refreshTrackedGraph` of `runtime/memory/v2/query.ts`
     walks each written document again under each selector the tracker holds for
     it (`rewalkDocument`, `evaluateTrackedDocument`), and a walk follows the
     links the selector's schema lets it follow. On the generated Topics boards
     the subscription is the harness's and not the piece's: each topic is a cell
     made under a schema that declares a label and no structure (`topicSchemaOf`
     of `compare/topics/scale.ts`), which admits every link, so the walk of
     topic `k` follows its mentions to the topics before it and reads `k + 3`
     documents, 2, 34 and 63 reads for the first, the middle and the last of 60
     topics. The piece reads through transactions and holds no query. With the
     mentions declared as references in that schema, a write of a field the
     board does not read takes 12, 8 and 14 ms at the first, the middle and the
     last of 2,000 topics, where it takes 25, 44 and 79 ms under the schema with
     no structure. On a real board the cost is the number of documents reachable
     through links from the written document under the schema of the widest
     query that reaches it: the topic itself where topics are read under the
     board's argument schema, which declares the mentions as cells, and the
     transitive closure of the topic's mentions for a reader that subscribes
     with no schema or with one that declares no structure. It is on today's
     path as well. No real board was measured. *The plan, not built:* a write
     that changes no link of the written document leaves what the walk reaches
     as it is, so the refresh sends the document's own snapshot, keeps the
     closure, and walks again only where a link was added or removed; and a walk
     that reaches a document already tracked under a selector that covers the
     one it arrives with stops there, which `coveringSelector` decides for the
     roots. *Assumed:* a cost of the memory server that this work does not
     change; each figure says which topic schema it was measured under.
370. **The constructs that Topics needs, so that a create and an edit of the
     mentions do not read the whole board** (answered in part: by the ruling Z87
     the constructs are designed and built; their surface is question 382, and
     what still follows the board is question 379). With the three whole-list
     `lift`s `namesTable`, `crossrefTable` and `crossrefIndexOf`, a create and
     an edit of a topic's mentions or `shortName` read every topic. Measured on
     the board `filing-order` on 2026-11-22 at 100, 1,000 and 2,000 topics, with
     the mentions declared as references in the harness's topic schema: a create
     takes 158, 1,034 and 1,783 ms and reads 2,061, 19,161 and 38,161 positions;
     an edit of the mentions takes 34, 273 and 517 ms and reads 1,000, 10,000
     and 20,000 positions; an edit of the `shortName` takes 44, 365 and 773 ms;
     and on `sorted-references` an edit of `lastActivityAt` runs the sorting
     `lift` over every topic, 57, 445 and 868 ms. *What is built* (provisional
     decisions P67 to P86; the integration plan, "The constructs"): (a) the
     per-entry construct over a record is `Object.entries(record).map(f)` over a
     record that is an input, keyed by the entry's name, and not a source
     `entries(record)`; (b) the keyed join is a `map` whose body calls `lookup`
     in an index, with a `flatMap` into pairs for a source that names several
     keys, and not a function `joinBy`; (c) the grouping is the method
     `groupBy`, with `keyBy` and `lookup`, which the language and today's
     runtime have, and its result is a collection index and not a record; and
     the sort is the method `sortBy`. *A correction of the label rule first
     proposed for the join:* a row has the label of the key of every source, of
     those that are in no bucket of the row as well, since an absent match is an
     observation of every key; the rule that a source that names no key of a row
     adds nothing to the row was an under-label.
     *Measured on the boards on the constructs,* on 2026-11-23 under the same
     schema, with a row that holds its bucket by a link and the kept indexes
     stored bucket by bucket, the median of three runs: an edit of the mentions
     takes 18, 23 and 26 ms on `filing-order` and reads 4 positions at every
     size; an edit of the `shortName` takes 18, 27 and 386 ms, the 386 ms
     holding a pause of the harness's own write; an edit of `lastActivityAt` on
     `sorted-references` 18, 52 and 81 ms; and a create 98, 279 and 547 ms with
     57 positions read and 102 records at every size. Every step reads and
     records the same at each size. The time of a create and of a move in the
     sorted order follows the board: each writes a document that holds a list of
     links, which costs in proportion to the document in the runtime itself
     (questions 379, 424 and 425).
     *Assumed:* the constructs as built. The label rules are the build
     agents' reading of `plan-and-label-templates.md` §3.17 and are not reviewed
     against the specification (questions 391 to 401 and 405 to 411).
371. **The executor compares every unit of the result in each derivation** (not
     for the owner). The piece's own time in an edit of a title on
     `sorted-references` is 2.9, 4.5 and 5.6 ms at 100, 1,000 and 2,000 topics.
     A profile of one edit at 2,000 topics has 4.5 of 7.5 ms in
     `Instance.#storeUnit` under `Instance.#storeResult`, 2.3 ms of them in
     `canonical` of `exec/store.ts`: each derivation stores every unit of the
     result again and compares what it holds member by member, and the result of
     this board holds the output of `topicsByActivity`, an array of one
     reference for each topic, where `filing-order` holds no such array.
     *Assumed:* a cost of the build and no change of what is stored. *The plan,
     not built:* a unit whose entry was not evaluated in the derivation is not
     compared.
372. **What milestones 3 and 6 leave before a compiled piece can stand in for
     today's** (not for the owner).
     A piece is set up by a client, compiled and run by a serving runtime, and
     resumed from what it stored, and a pattern is started from its source
     through `Runtime.run` where a runtime is given a compiler. A document that
     is not in the replica reads as absent on a runtime that does not read from
     the store, and a document of another space that the replica does not hold
     is not brought. The runtime does not follow a link whose path crosses an
     array by key, which the rows of a `map` over an array of plain values in
     place hold, and reads a state cell with no document as nothing where the
     executor reads the default of its schema. The shell does not render a
     compiled piece. Of the corpus, 183 of 239 modules run pass on the runner
     path and under the serving loop, and 182 after a resume (questions 376 and
     437).
     Value code
     runs in a compartment, and the crate's check is what keeps a body inside
     its footprint (question 386). The board `main` and the rows-in-place layout
     were not measured with the reads through handles, the label readers or the
     constructs, today's arm was not run at 2,000 topics or beside the boards on
     the constructs, which it does not take, and no figure is of two writers or
     of an idle machine. *Assumed:* each is a stub with its reason in the
     integration plan, and the figures of the milestones are read with them. The
     order in which they are built is not decided.
373. **Whether the first derivation of an instance a handler made may be a
     transaction of its own** (settled by the ruling Z87 of 2026-11-22: it
     may; provisional decision P64 stands). The derivation behind an event
     that made an instance is two transactions: the first derives the new
     instance alone and is committed, and the second derives what reads it.
     Each derivation is evaluated once. A reader between the two finds the
     new member with its result and the board's derived outputs without it.
     *Open:* the sentences of `execution-and-storage.md` §1.1 and §1.4 and of
     `scheduler-and-serving-loop.md` ("Terms", §5.2, §5.4) that say one
     derivation transaction runs behind the batch are brought in line.
374. **What the load in bounded transactions leaves** (not for the owner;
     provisional decision P65; beside question 368). First, where the caller
     does not commit the handed transaction, or its commit is refused, the
     creation and the row documents that the load committed stay stored, with
     sound labels and with no document that links to them, and nothing removes
     them. No test covers it. Second, the documents a `lift` writes for its rows
     are given their records when the body has returned, and stay in the handed
     transaction: 4,000 of the 8,011 documents at 2,000 topics, so a board of
     about twice that size is refused by the memory server as a load in one
     commit is at 2,000. Third, the commits of the adapter keep
     `StorageManager.synced()` waiting like any commit, so a harness that
     withholds the server's fan-out loads with `loadRows` set to `Infinity`, as
     `refused-commit.test.ts` does. *Assumed:* as built; a board past the limit
     is loaded with the memory server's limit raised in the harness. *Open:*
     what removes the documents of a load whose handed transaction did not
     commit, and how a row that a `lift` writes is stored apart when its record
     is given after the body has returned.
375. **A load written into one transaction over-labels what is bound through the
     argument** (not for the owner until examined). On Topics boards of 6 topics
     with a clause per topic, of 4,652 probes of what a read of the result
     consumes over the load, three edits and three creates, the load in bounded
     transactions gives the same as the load in one transaction at 4,546 and
     less at 106, on both boards, and more at none. The 106 are at `topics`,
     `names`, `namesTable` and `index`, whose records are bound through the
     argument document. In a load in one transaction that document is staged,
     and a staged document takes the join of everything the transaction read, so
     each of the four holds the clause of the other input; with the creation
     stored first they hold the label of the reference alone. A load into a
     transaction the caller wrote into, and one with `loadRows` set to
     `Infinity`, are written whole and have it, and so has every figure of a
     load in one commit. *Assumed:* an over-label and no under-label; the load
     in bounded transactions is the default. Not examined beyond the 106 probes.
376. **The corpus on the runner path** (not for the owner).
     `compare/runner-corpus.ts` runs the main pattern of each module as a
     compiled piece, with the generated inputs as plain values and the generated
     events queued with the scheduler, and beside it on the executor in memory.
     With no table for a `wish`: of 373 modules, 134 are not run (66 export no
     pattern, 40 need `wish`, 24 request an effect, 4 have no value code) and
     239 are run: 230 start with the first commit taken, 200 handle every event,
     215 have no commit refused, 210 hold the values the executor in memory
     holds, with the members of each record ordered, and 183 do all four. With a
     `wish` answered from the table of a seeded home (P197), 272 of 375 modules
     are run: 258 start, 219 handle every event, 248 have no commit refused and
     228 hold the values of the executor in memory. The classes that follow are
     of the run with no table.
     Of the 9 that do not start, the value
     code throws in 4, the executor lacks the built-ins `indexedCollections`,
     `getEntityId` and `linksOf` in a function body in 1 each, and the
     preparation refuses the first commit for a `writeAuthorizedBy` claim that
     no template covers in 2. Of the 30 with an event not handled, 23 have no
     stream of the binding stored, because the binding is in an element body
     whose collection has no element or the stream belongs to an instance a body
     made, and in 7 the handler did not commit. Of the 15 with a commit refused:
     a missing trusted-event policy input, 6; the transaction aborted, 5;
     `writeAuthorizedBy`, 1; `maxConfidentiality`, 2; a writer-fit misfit, 1. In
     7 modules the values differ with every event handled and no commit refused;
     they are not examined, and a draw of the random source or of the clock in
     an event differs between the two runs by construction. The comparison is
     with the executor in memory and not with today's runtime, and the inputs
     are plain values, so the run says little about labels. *Assumed:* each
     class is a gap of the build with its cause named, but for the 7, which are
     assumed to be defects until examined.
377. **An edit of the last of 2,000 topics that takes 256 to 265 ms** (not for
     the owner until examined). On both boards, in three runs, with the mentions
     declared as references, the edit of the title of the last of 2,000 topics
     takes 256 to 265 ms, with 7 ms of preparation and 2 to 4 ms in the piece,
     where every other edit of a title takes 9 to 17 ms. A write alone at the
     middle of 1,000 topics took 143 ms once. The cause was not looked for.
     These figures are of the boards with the three `lift`s. On the boards on
     the constructs the same edit takes 10 to 16 ms in three runs of each
     board, and pauses of 170 to 220 ms that the piece and the preparation do
     not account for were seen, in one trace and one profile, to be a
     mark-compact collection and an insertion into the weak set of deep-frozen
     objects (question 383). The edit of this question was not profiled.
     *Assumed:* a cost outside the piece and the preparation, until examined.
378. **The harness switches of the Topics tables** (settled). The Topics
     scale harness with every switch the tables of milestone 3 name,
     `SCALE_TOPIC_SCHEMA=mentions-as-cells` among them, is on the branch of
     milestone 3 (`base/pattern-compiler/compare/topics/scale.ts`). The boards
     `board-filing-order.tsx` and `board-sorted-references.tsx` that the
     tables measure are on the local branch
     `claude/compiled-pattern-topics-runs`, with the compiled subset of
     Topics, which is a change to a pattern and so not part of the stack.
     *Open:* where those two boards go (question 382).

**From the constructs of milestone 3 and from milestone 5 (2026-11-22 and
2026-11-23).** The constructs that stand in the place of Topics' whole-list
`lift`s are built and the two boards are written with them, and value code runs
in a compartment
([compiled-pattern-language-integration.md](compiled-pattern-language-integration.md),
"Milestone 3: a compiled piece in the runner" and "Milestone 5: value code in
the sandbox"). Questions 370, 372, 377 and 378 above are brought in line with
it. The provisional decisions P67 to P86 and P100 to P103 are of this work.
Whenever a question says `map`, `filter`, `flatMap`, `groupBy` or `sortBy`, it
names the case.

379. **An array of the result stored so that one change writes no document that
     grows with the data** (not for the owner until designed; provisional
     decisions P69, P88 and P90). For a kept index this is built: each bucket is
     a document of its own, the stored index holds no array of its occupied
     keys, and a change of one member's key writes two bucket documents and two
     links (P88); an edit of a `shortName` takes 20 and 35 ms at 100 and 1,000
     topics where it took 42 and 275. What is left is every list of links in one
     document: the result document holds five (the three arrays of rows, the
     cards and the record of buckets), 0.81 MB at 1,000 topics, and a create
     appends to two inputs of 0.37 MB. A change of one link of such a document
     costs in proportion to the document in the runtime itself (question 424), a
     move in an array of links is written as the array (question 425), and an
     append writes a document as long as the list. *The plan, not built:* the
     part documents of P20 (`exec/parts.ts`), which the runner path runs
     without; for the index, `keys()` and `keyEntries()`, which would read the
     names of the members of the record of buckets. *Open:* whether the label of
     the membership is stored once for the index (P69; question 394) or in each
     bucket document (question 406); and whether part documents wait for the
     storage layer, as "The scope of the storage decisions" has it. *Assumed:*
     as built, with the cost stated.
380. **The key of a plain value that holds references** (not for the owner until
     designed; provisional decisions P76 and P92). For a member of a stored
     array this is built: a member that holds links is keyed by its own content
     with each link as the address of what it names, and nothing is read of what
     is stored there (P92). It closed a defect: a `map` over such values lost
     every row when a document a reference leads to was written. *What is left:*
     `Instance.#table` of `exec/executor.ts` keys a plain value of an array that
     no document holds by the salted hash of the value with every reference
     followed; no fixture reaches it with a value that holds a reference, and
     nothing in the crate refuses one. The members of a bucket are exempt (P76).
     *Open:* the keys of stored values that hold links changed with P92, and
     with them the identity of what is derived for each; the ruling on the
     salted hash of a plain value says nothing of a link inside the value. Its
     label side is question 400. *Assumed:* as built.
381. **A handler that is handed a collection reads it whole** (not for the
     owner; provisional decisions P81 and P91). For a function body this is
     built in the executor: nothing is read of the computed part of the argument
     at a path that an entry of `Body.reads` fills (P91), so the `lift`
     `backlinksOf` of a new topic, which declares the pivot and its index as
     cells, reads the one bucket it asks for,
     and a create reads 57 positions at every size, with the `enumeration` entry
     of a handler's state read with no link of a child followed (P141).
     *What is left:* the executor hands a
     handler each value it closes over, read whole (`Instance.#attempt`), so the
     verb `addTopic` is a handler with cells in its state, and any `action` that
     passes a collection on to an instance it makes has the cost. *The plan, not
     built:* the crate observes a captured value that the body only passes on as
     `identity`, and gives a parameter declared as a cell no `value` entry,
     where the executor leaves the computed part unread. *Assumed:* as built.
382. **The surface of the constructs, and that the two measured boards do not
     run on today's runtime** (for the owner; provisional decisions P67, P68,
     P70, P80 and P85). The ruling Z87 has the three constructs that Topics
     lacks designed and built next; which surface they have was the
     coordinator's to choose and is the owner's to ratify. As built: the
     grouping is `groupBy` and `keyBy` with `lookup`, which the language and
     today's runtime have; the keyed join is a `map` whose body calls `lookup`,
     with a `flatMap` into pairs for a source that names several keys; the
     per-entry construct is `Object.entries(record).map`; and the sort is a new
     method `sortBy`, ascending, with texts ordered by their code units and not
     by `localeCompare`. *What follows for today's path:* `base/api/index.ts`
     declares `groupBy` on a cell of an array and no `sortBy`, so a grouping of
     the result of another per-element construct and every `sortBy` are in the
     compiled language alone, and the boards `board-filing-order.tsx` and
     `board-sorted-references.tsx` run on the runner path and not on today's
     runtime. The two boards differ from the boards with the three `lift`s in
     three observable points: a topic the board lists at two entries has two
     rows of the pivot, a key of the namespace that the name grammar does not
     admit has a row of the table, and a topic whose sort key reads as
     `undefined` has a card behind every other. *Open:* whether `sortBy`, and
     `groupBy` over the result of a per-element construct, are added to
     `base/api/index.ts` with a lowering in today's transformer, so that one
     source runs both ways; whether texts sort by code units; whether a
     descending order gets a form of its own; and where the two boards go, which
     question 378 leaves open. *The coordinator's recommendation, not a
     ruling:* the surface as built, and the two methods added to today's API
     before a board on the constructs goes to `main`. *Assumed* until answered:
     as built.
383. **Measurements of the Topics boards on the constructs that are not
     explained or not made** (not for the owner until examined). A create at
     2,000 topics on `filing-order` took 2,174 ms and 3,323 ms in two
     measurements of 2026-11-22 with the same reads; a run of the later code on
     2026-11-23 has 3,579 ms with 1,303 ms in the piece. The difference is not
     explained beyond this: a create at 2,000 topics allocates past the heap's
     limit and takes a major collection in some runs and not in others. With the
     argument of a body read once it takes 1,371 to 1,580 ms. Three cells of the
     tables of 2026-11-23 are a pause in the harness's own write, one call of
     `deepFreeze` of `base/data-model/src/deep-freeze.ts` that grows the weak
     set of deep-frozen objects, 291 of 353 ms in one profile; and one trace of
     2026-11-22 has a mark-compact collection of 181 ms at a heap of 1.1 GB.
     With a row that holds its bucket by a link a create takes 98, 279 and 547
     ms. Not made: a profile of
     `sorted-references`; a run under the default schema with the buckets as
     documents; a run with a clause for each topic; a run of the boards with the
     two evaluators of milestone 5 compared; a run of today's runtime at these
     sizes beside them; more than three runs for each cell, and a machine with
     no other load. *Assumed:* costs outside the piece and the preparation,
     until examined. Question 377 is the same for the boards with the three
     `lift`s.
384. **What the constructs do not cover** (not for the owner). Each is a gap of
     the build with its cause named. `keys()` and `keyEntries()` of an index are
     not built. A `lookup` by a cell in an index the instance is handed, and a
     key whose type the crate does not resolve, are listed as unsupported; the
     crate does not resolve the type of a row of a `map` written in the body of
     a `flatMap`, so the parameter of a key function over such rows is
     annotated. The executor forms the record of a kept index whole for each
     change of a bucket, though the storage is written for the buckets that
     changed alone (P88), and `Index` finds a member in its bucket by a scan, so
     the time of a change of a key follows the size of the two buckets: 8.7 ms
     at 10,000 members in ten buckets. A `sortBy` and a `filter` over the result
     of another per-element construct form their order whole for each change,
     158 ms for one change among 16,000 elements, and a `sortBy` over an array
     of references does so when an element moved in the source. A `flatMap`
     whose body returns a stored array or writes one, and any `flatMap` after a
     change of its source array, forms its assembly whole. `Object.keys(x).map`,
     `Object.values(x).map` and a `filter` or a `flatMap` over the entries of a
     record stay expressions over the whole record, and the element table of
     `Object.entries(x).map` is formed again for each change of the record. A
     record whose entry a handler removes and adds again under one name within a
     transaction keeps the row's state, as a re-keyed element does under the
     ruling Z41. The plan of an index holds no `Operation` record (P72).
     *Assumed:* each as built; none is needed by the two Topics boards.
385. **Over-labels of the constructs** (not for the owner; noted under the
     ruling Z88 and not resolved). The name of a row of
     `Object.entries(record).map` whose rows are in place is bound to no stored
     position and takes the join of the transaction that derived the row; the
     plan is to bind the slot of the name to the record's `enumeration`. The
     `name` of the result of a second piece that is handed a kept index consumes
     the clause of every item beside its own; not examined, and the crate reads
     the handed index with `$h.read` and no slot. Where a bucket holds copies of
     rows, its label is joined with the fold of the row's template over the
     source, an over-label of each bucket by the rows of the others. On the two
     boards the rows of `namesTable` are documents, since the boards declare the
     values of `names` as cells (P78 and P87). A bucket document written after
     the load stores the join of what its transaction read (question 407), and a
     splice written as the array joins the label of the array into the writes
     under no record (question 410). *Assumed:* none is an under-label.
386. **What keeps a function body inside its footprint by the crate's check
     alone** (for the owner, as to what has to be closed before a compiled
     piece runs a pattern that is not trusted; provisional decisions P100, P112
     and P170 to P172). The compartment confines names. The emitted text
     freezes module data and hardens functions (P170), what a handle names is
     in private fields (P171), and the check refuses a member of a handle that
     the language does not list, a write to a listed one, and a declaration of
     a name that begins with `$` (P172). `emit` prints no artifact for a
     refused module unless `--unchecked` asks, and the serving loader of
     milestone 6 evaluates no artifact it did not compile (P110). *Open, on the
     check alone:* the emitted text binds `$rt`, `$h`, `$arg`, `$e` and `$s`
     around authored code; `Host.slot` reads whatever slot of the plan it is
     given and counts it without refusing, and a `Host` is not frozen. *Open,
     on nothing:* a body that catches an error the executor threw reads its
     members, the error state of the value whose read failed among them; and a
     body that narrows a value typed `unknown` and finds the stand-in of a
     reference reads the identifier of its document (questions 443 and 444).
     *The plan, not built:* the host as an object with private state that is
     handed to authored code through no name, which changes the shape of the
     emitted code. *The coordinator's recommendation, not a ruling:* that
     before the option is on for a space that holds a pattern of another
     author, with the other items of question 434. *Assumed* until answered:
     the check, on a path that is off by default and a measurement.
387. **The start of a pattern from its source through `Runtime.run`, and the two
     decisions it needed** (for the owner; provisional decisions P101, P110,
     P111 and P173 to P176). With a compiler given to a runtime
     (`runCompiledPatterns`), `PatternManager.compilePattern` hands the program
     to it and `Runner.run` starts a compiled piece where the program is
     accepted. *The two decisions, made provisionally:* a program the crate
     refuses runs on today's path with the diagnostics logged, and a resume
     whose program is no longer accepted is refused with the reason stored (P175
     and P176); and a stored piece names the entity of its program text, with no
     compiler build in it (P174), where `scheduler-and-serving-loop.md` §10.5
     has the result cell name the hash of the `CompiledPattern` record. *Open
     with it:* the mark of a compiled space is not built, and nothing gives a
     toolshed's runtime a compiler; §10.5 has compiling run in the compile
     worker with the instance unloaded meanwhile, where the loader awaits a
     child process inside the loop's start of the piece. What the path leaves is
     question 468. *Assumed:* as built behind a helper of tests.
388. **A function body that is handed a whole array is handed a copy of it for
     each call** (not for the owner; provisional decisions P91 and P179). For a
     `lift` over an array of plain values in place, 14 of the 27 ms of one edit
     at 10,000 rows on the executor in memory are the read of the array, a copy
     that gives each record an address (`Store.read`), and the rest is
     `Host.pass`, which copies the argument again, and the walk of the result.
     For a `map` over the same array, whose element body reads one row, the edit
     costs 0.3 ms. The array is read once for a call (P91), and the keys of a
     whole read are kept (P179). The read stays a copy while a body may change
     what it is handed and while the store changes stored containers in place.
     *The plan, not built:* a write that copies the containers on the path to
     what it changes; the address of a stored container kept by the store for
     its position; a read under no schema, of a container that holds no link and
     needs no default, that returns the stored container; a read through a
     handle in a body kept a copy; and the corpus run both ways, since a body
     that sorts its argument in place would fail. On FabriChat a read that
     copies is 115 ms of a send of 257 ms in memory at 1,000 messages.
     *Assumed:* a cost of the build.
389. **What milestone 5 leaves unmeasured and unbuilt beside the two above**
     (not for the owner; P177 and P178). No claim keeps two processes from
     compiling one source at once; both write the same text. The compile has no
     bound on its time, and no test stops one by its signal. An edit in a `map`
     over an array of plain values in place does work that follows the length of
     the array, 0.08 ms at 1,000 and at 10,000 rows, and that work is about four
     times slower in a realm that is locked down, 0.30 ms at 10,000; which step
     it is was not profiled. The runner path was measured in three runs for each
     cell on a loaded machine, and its arms do not separate. The freeze of
     module data exists twice, in the executor and in the runner's sandbox. No
     continuous-integration job builds the binary, and no WebAssembly build
     exists for where no native binary can run. *Assumed:* each as built.
390. **Statements of the design's documents that the provisional decisions P67
     to P92, P100 to P103, P110 to P120, P130 to P136, P140 to P153, P170 to
     P179 and P190 to P210 differ from** (not for
     the owner; a list for the author who brings the documents in line, and none
     is changed here). `plan-and-label-templates.md` §1.1 lists the values of
     `construct` and of `source.via` without `groupBy`, `keyBy` and `sortBy`,
     and has a bucket of an index as a source of kind `operation`; §3.17 has the
     index as an `Operation` of kind `index` (P72), reads as a label entry for
     each bucket (P69), and says nothing of a bucket over the result of another
     per-element construct or of a copied row (P67, P77); no section has a
     `Collection` over the entries of a record with `source.entries` and element
     paths `0` and `1` (P70), a sort by a key (P85), a slot bound to an output
     and to a read at once (P74), or the segments of a `flatMap` (P84).
     `language-subset.md` §4.4 lists the collection methods and the index
     methods without `sortBy`, and has `toSorted` with a comparator as
     function-tier code (P85); §4.4.1 shows `Object.entries(prices).map` as a
     destructuring example and not as a per-entry construct with the entry's
     name as the element key (P70); §9 lists `localeCompare`, which the order of

     says the compiler's check is the only
     one, which holds only for an artifact of `emit --accepted`, and that the

     a plain value keyed by a salted hash of its content, it has no case of a

     `scheduler-and-serving-loop.md` §10.5 has compiling run in the compile

     `builtin-inventory.md` has `groupBy` and `keyBy` as class A with durable

     `execution-and-storage.md` has a plain value keyed by a salted hash of its

     each link as the address it names (P92); and no document has a splice of a

     P130 to P136,* in `scheduler-and-serving-loop.md`: §10.2 has one derivation
     transaction behind the batch, where the derivation is one effect of the
     scheduler and the load is a transaction of a wave (P134); §10.4 has basis
     rows of a cone instance and a document, written by the memory server in the
     store transaction of the wave, where the basis is one document of the piece
     with its numbers in 256 parts, written by the piece in a transaction of its
     derivation, with a list of sources whose number is not known (P113 to P116
     and P120), and §10.6 has stale cone instances marked at activation, where a

     each path and a read answered from the rows, where demand on any document
     of a piece loads the piece; §10.5 has the instance stay unloaded with its
     demand pending while the compile worker compiles, the compiled pattern

     and its delivery to clients, where the loader awaits a child process inside

     stores a reason where it refuses (P110 and P111); §5.1 has stream

     §5.5 has a conflict leave out the derived write that conflicts,
     where the piece restores every document the withdrawn transaction wrote
     (P135); §10.3 has the acting principal, the scope key and the read ceiling
